summary: Defines MIB objects, extending the Entity MIB from RFC 2737, for generalized access to information about physical sensors in network equipment, such as chassis temperature, fan speed and power supply voltage.

eli5.summary: Network boxes have thermometers and fan meters inside. This note gives a standard way for a manager to read them remotely.

questions: what is the entity sensor mib
how to read temperature with snmp
subtitle: A standard SNMP table for reading temperature, fan speed, voltage and other sensors inside network equipment.

tldr.problem: Network equipment contains physical sensors such as chassis temperature, fan RPM and power supply voltage, but there was no standard way to read them remotely.
tldr.mechanism: The ENTITY-SENSOR-MIB adds one table, entPhySensorTable, that extends the Entity MIB. Each sensor row carries a type, a scale, a precision, a value, a status and update information.
tldr.outcome: A manager can read any kind of sensor in a consistent way. No thresholds or alarms are defined; the RFC points to the RMON Alarm and Event groups for that.

today: RFC 3433 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the ENTITY-SENSOR-MIB as published in December 2002.

sections.title: Why a Sensor MIB
sections.content:
RFC 3433 defines a MIB module, ENTITY-SENSOR-MIB, for use with network management protocols. It extends the Entity MIB of RFC 2737 to give generalized access to information about the physical sensors found in networking equipment. Examples given are chassis temperature, fan RPM and power supply voltage.

The information to expose is the current value, the operational status, and the units and precision of the reading, in a consistent form for any type of sensor. The MIB is written in SMIv2, as described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580, and objects are generally accessed through SNMP. The overall framework is described in RFC 3410.
sections.eli5: Many boxes have gauges inside, but each maker shows them differently. This document says how everyone should show them so one tool can read all of them.

sections.title: How It Attaches to the Entity MIB
sections.content:
A physical sensor is already represented in the Entity MIB by an entPhysicalEntry whose entPhysicalClass is sensor(8). This MIB is a sparse augmentation of the entPhysicalTable: it adds extra information only for rows that are sensors, and uses the same entPhysicalIndex as the index.

An agent is expected to keep one entPhySensorEntry for each such sensor row. Because of that, implementing the entityPhysicalGroup is required for agents that implement the Entity Sensor MIB. Entries are created by the agent, SHOULD be created together with the matching entPhysicalEntry, and SHOULD be destroyed when it is.

There is one group, entitySensorValueGroup, and one table, entPhySensorTable, and all its objects are read-only.
sections.eli5: The Entity MIB is a list of every part in the box. This MIB adds a gauge reading beside each part that is a sensor.

sections.title: The Sensor Table Objects
sections.content:
Each row has eight read-only objects: entPhySensorType (the kind of units), entPhySensorScale (a power-of-10 scaling factor), entPhySensorPrecision (decimal places), entPhySensorValue (the current reading), entPhySensorOperStatus, entPhySensorUnitsDisplay (a text description of the units), entPhySensorValueTimeStamp and entPhySensorValueUpdateRate.

The type, scale and precision SHOULD be set by the agent when the entry is created and SHOULD NOT change during operation. To interpret the value you must read all three together with it.

The update rate is in milliseconds. A value of zero means the value is updated on demand, updated when it changes (event-driven), or that the agent does not know the update rate. The timestamp holds sysUpTime at the last time the agent obtained the value.
sections.eli5: Each gauge reports what it measures, the size of the number, how exact it is, the reading itself, and whether it is working.

sections.title: Types, Scales and Precision
sections.content:
The sensor type is one of twelve values: other, unknown, voltsAC, voltsDC, amperes, watts, hertz, celsius, percentRH, rpm, cmm (cubic meters per minute) and truthvalue. The scale uses SI prefixes from yocto(1), meaning 10^-24, up to yotta(17), meaning 10^24, with units(9) as 10^0.

Precision is an Integer32 from -8 to 9. A value from 1 to 9 is the number of decimal places in the fixed-point value. A value from -8 to -1 is the number of accurate digits. Zero means the value is not a fixed-point number.

The RFC's example is a temperature sensor measuring 0 to 100 degrees C in 0.1 degree steps. It has precision 1, scale units(9), and a value from 0 to 1000, read as degrees C times 10.

For the electrical, hertz, celsius and cmm types, the value is a fixed-point number from -999,999,999 to +999,999,999. The value -1000000000 means underflow and +1000000000 means overflow. For percentRH it ranges from 0 to 100.
sections.eli5: A reading of 253 could mean 25.3 degrees. Precision says where the decimal point goes, and scale says whether it is in units, thousands, or millionths.

sections.title: Sensor Status and Thresholds
sections.content:
The operational status has three values. ok(1) means the agent can obtain the sensor value. unavailable(2) means it presently cannot. nonoperational(3) means the agent believes the sensor is broken, through a hard failure such as a disconnected wire or a soft failure such as out-of-range, jittery or wildly fluctuating readings.

No special thresholding is defined in this MIB. The RFC recommends a generalized thresholding MIB instead, such as the Alarm and Events groups of the Remote Network Monitoring MIB, RFC 2819.
sections.eli5: A gauge can say it is fine, that it cannot be read right now, or that it looks broken. Warning alarms are left to other tools.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
One object may contain sensitive information: entPhySensorValue, because it may expose the values of particular physical sensors of a device. The RFC says SNMPv1 by itself is not a secure environment, and that even a secured network gives no control over who may access the objects.

Implementors are urged to consider the SNMPv3 security features, specifically the User-based Security Model (RFC 3414) and the View-based Access Control Model (RFC 3415). It is the customer's or user's responsibility to configure the SNMP entity so that only legitimate principals can access these objects.
sections.eli5: Anyone who can read the gauges learns about the box, so only the right people should be allowed to look.
